headline: 71.2°F at the Bight, Warm Filament Holds — Yellowfin and Mahi Keep Coming on the Troll
subhead: A stable warm-water tongue is still sitting over the canyon edge, and the fleet working the 100-fathom line, the Claw, and the Dip is cashing in before the moon and the tropics have a say.
body_markdown:
71.2°F. That's the reading off buoy 44025 out in the Bight this week, with seas running 3 to 4 feet on a short 5-second period — nothing dramatic, but it tells you the surface layer is stable and the ride out hasn't been beating anybody up too badly. That number by itself isn't the story. The story is what's sitting on top of it: a warm filament pushing off the Gulf Stream that's been parked over the canyon edge for close to two weeks now, and it hasn't budged. We flagged this last week — said the pattern would hold through several more days of stable high pressure before any wind shift or cool front started pushing on that warm edge — and that's exactly what's played out. No front has come through to knock it loose, and the fleet radioing in from the sword grounds and the tuna spreads is backing that up.

Yellowfin have been the most consistent player, and they're doing it the way late-August yellowfin usually do out here — working the color change and temp breaks along the 100-fathom line and pushing up onto the Claw when the current sets up right. Green machines and small Ilanders in the spreader bar, cedar plugs way back, and naked ballyhoo skipped off the corner have all been drawing strikes. Fish in the 20 to 40-pound class have been the bulk of it, with the occasional bigger one mixed in on the chunk once the trolling bite shuts down around midday. That's the pattern worth knowing — troll the break in the morning, then switch over to butterfish chunks anchored up or drifting near structure like the Dip once the sun gets high and the fish stop chasing iron.

Bluefin have been mixed in on some of those chunk drops, not consistent enough to call a sure thing but enough that boats are keeping a rod rigged with a 50 or 80-wide and a fresh butterfish chunk soaking on a slow current. Mahi have been scattered around any floating structure — weed lines, debris, current seams where the warm water meets slightly cooler green — and small skirted ballyhoo or dink feathers pulled just off the temp break have been picking them off, mostly schoolies in the 3 to 8-pound range with the occasional bull mixed in near actual structure.

White marlin have shown consistently enough on the dink spread and naked ballyhoo pulled flat lines that it's worth running one dedicated teaser and a couple of light baits even on a tuna-focused spread. Nothing has been stacked wall to wall — this is a "keep working the temp break and stay ready" bite, not a "set it and forget it" one. Boats that ran the edge without adjusting to where the color and the break actually sat some mornings came back with a quieter day than the ones that worked the grid and found where bait was actually getting pushed up.

Swordfish have still been down deep during daylight, which hasn't changed with the season. Boats running daytime drops with squid strips and glow rigs on electric reels down in that 1,500 to 1,800-foot range have connected, though it's a grind — long soaks, patient drops, and reading the sound machine for that bottom layer of bait before committing a full drop. Worth the setup time if that's the target, but it's not a fast bite by any measure.

Here's the honest part: this bite depends entirely on that warm filament staying put, and the moon is about to complicate things. As it builds toward full over the next several days, expect tidal flow to increase and bait to start concentrating tighter around structure — which can actually help the canyon bite by pulling forage up onto the edge, but it also means current lines can shift fast and the color break that produced Tuesday might not be sitting in the same spot Friday. Run the SST overlay before you leave the dock, don't assume last week's numbers hold, and be ready to make a move of five or ten miles if the first pass over the 100-fathom line comes up quiet.

The bigger wildcard heading into Labor Day weekend is tropical activity. Peak hurricane season doesn't care about a good bite, and any system spinning up in the western Atlantic can push swell and mix that warm surface layer down before anyone gets a forecast update. As of now there's nothing forcing a change, and the pattern that's held through stable high pressure all month looks likely to carry through the next few days. Expect more boat traffic over the holiday weekend as word spreads that the canyon's producing, so get an early start if crowding on the good stretches of the edge is a concern. If the filament holds and the moon doesn't scatter the bait too hard, the next few days should look a lot like the last two weeks — yellowfin on the troll in the morning, chunk bite for bluefin and stragglers midday, and mahi wherever the debris and the color line up. Watch the storm tracks closely. That's still the single biggest thing that can end this run.
